blocks.text: This is where everything from this module comes together. One assistant, three MCP servers, one real request.
We will connect a database server, a search server, and a calendar server to the same host, and watch one user ask get handled end to end.
Along the way we revisit how the assistant picks the right tool for each step, and what it takes to keep three live connections healthy.
1. The Request We Are Building Toward
Say a user asks: schedule a follow up with our top customer and email me a summary before the meeting.
No single tool answers that. It needs a database lookup, a bit of web context, and a calendar action, in order.
That is exactly the shape of task this module has been building toward all along.
2. Three Servers, One Host

blocks.alt: A user request flows through a host into a database server, a search server, and a calendar server

blocks.text: The host is the single program the user talks to. It is not the database server or the calendar server itself.
Instead, the host holds three separate MCP client connections, one to each server, and merges what they offer.

items: Database server, exposes tools like query_customers and get_order_history.
Search server, exposes a web_search tool for fresh outside context.
Calendar server, exposes find_free_slot and create_event.

blocks.text: 3. Aggregating the Tool List

blocks.alt: Tools from three servers aggregate into one combined list for the model

blocks.text: Before the assistant can act, the host asks each server what it can do, using tools/list on every connection.
The three answers get merged into one combined list that the model sees as a single menu of options.
Prefixing each tool name with its server name avoids collisions if two servers ever expose a tool with the same short name.
This merge step happens once per session, or whenever a server connects or disconnects, not on every single user message.
4. Deciding Which Tool Handles Which Part
This is dynamic tool routing in practice. The model looks at the aggregated list and the current step of the plan.
It is not told in code to use the database server first, it infers that from the tool descriptions and the user request.
A request naming a customer routes toward query_customers. A request needing outside facts routes toward web_search.

blocks.title: Ties back to Dynamic Tool Routing
blocks.content: The routing logic here is the same idea covered earlier in this module, just applied across three live servers instead of one.

blocks.text: 5. Step One: Finding the Top Customer

blocks.alt: Step one finds the top customer, step two pulls context, step three books the meeting

blocks.text: The assistant first needs to know who the top customer actually is, so it reaches for the database server.
The model never wrote raw SQL. It called a named tool and got back a clean row of data to reason over.
6. Step Two: Pulling Fresh Context
Knowing the customer is Acme Corp, the assistant now wants something current to mention in the follow up.
This step exists purely because the database server cannot know what happened in the news today, only the search server can.
7. Step Three: Booking the Meeting
With a customer name and a talking point in hand, the assistant now checks the calendar for an open slot.
8. Combining Results Into One Answer

blocks.alt: Results from three separate steps combine into one final answer

blocks.text: None of the three tool results alone answers the user. The host has to stitch them into one reply.
The model takes the customer name, the news snippet, and the booked event, and writes a short human summary.

code.content:
Meeting booked with Acme Corp for Tuesday 10am.
They recently announced a new product line, worth mentioning
as a conversation opener. Calendar invite sent.

blocks.text: 9. Why Order Matters Here
Each step in this chain depends on the output of the one before it, so the assistant cannot run them all at once.
It needs the customer name before it can search, and it needs the search result before the calendar note makes sense.
Recognizing which steps are sequential and which could run in parallel is part of good routing, not just picking a tool name.
Independent steps, like checking two different database tables, can run at the same time to shave real seconds off the reply.
10. Keeping Track of Which Server Did What
With three servers in play, it helps to log which server answered which part of the request.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Server","Tool called","Result used for"],"rows":[["1","database","query_customers","Identifying the top customer"],["2","search","web_search","Finding a talking point"],["3","calendar","find_free_slot, create_event","Booking the meeting"]]}

blocks.text: This kind of trail makes debugging far easier when a user asks why the assistant said what it said.
11. Health Checks Across Three Connections

blocks.alt: A health check runs across all three server connections at once

blocks.text: Running three live connections means three things that can silently die mid conversation.
The host should ping each server periodically and mark a connection unhealthy before the model tries to use it.

items: Database server down, block query_customers and warn the user data may be stale.
Search server down, skip the news step rather than fail the whole request.
Calendar server down, hold off scheduling and tell the user to try again shortly.

blocks.text: 12. Permissions When Three Servers Share One User
Each server was built with its own idea of what a caller is allowed to do, and that does not automatically line up.
The database server might allow read only queries for this user, while the calendar server allows creating events but not deleting them.

blocks.title: Least privilege across servers
blocks.content: Grant the assistant only the scopes each server actually needs for this workflow, not the widest permission each server happens to offer.

blocks.text: 13. Cost of Running Three Servers at Once
Every tool call has a cost, both the API call itself and the tokens spent describing tools and results to the model.
Three servers means three sets of tool descriptions competing for context space on every single turn.
Trimming unused tools from the aggregated list before it reaches the model keeps both cost and confusion down.
14. What Happens When One Server Fails Mid Request

blocks.alt: One server failing mid request should not take down the other two

blocks.text: Suppose the calendar server times out right after the search step finished successfully.
A well built assistant does not throw away the customer name and news snippet it already gathered.
Reporting partial progress is more useful to the user than a bare error message.
15. Monitoring the Whole Assistant, Not Just One Server
Watching one server in isolation misses problems that only show up when three are combined.
Track end to end latency for the full request, not just each individual tool call, so a slow chain gets noticed.
16. Scaling Beyond Three Servers

blocks.alt: Three servers scaling up toward many more servers over time

blocks.text: Nothing about this pattern is capped at three servers, the same host logic works with five or ten.
What changes is the size of the aggregated tool list, and how much trimming and grouping it needs before reaching the model.
A good rule is to only connect the servers a given conversation is likely to need, rather than every server the user has access to.

Common Mistakes

items: Letting one slow server block the whole reply instead of returning partial results.
Giving the assistant the widest permission each server offers, instead of the least it actually needs.
Sending every tool from every server to the model on every turn, wasting context and money.
Not tagging which server produced which result, making failures hard to trace.
Assuming all three servers are always healthy and skipping any kind of connection check.
Running independent steps sequentially when they could safely run in parallel.

blocks.text: Practice
Sketch the tool call sequence for a request that needs an order history lookup, a shipping policy search, and a calendar reminder.
Then decide which of those three steps, if any, could safely run at the same time instead of one after another.
Key Takeaway
A multi tool assistant is not one big trick, it is the same small ideas from this module, aggregated tools, careful routing, health checks, permissions, and cost awareness, all running together.
